doc.title: Bernard Purdie interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Tape change; greed, missing melodies and rap hurting the industry
summary: After a tape change, Purdie says greed, songs without melodies and rap saturation damaged the music industry and shrank profits.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Listen, we need to change tapes here. Have you got another fifteen minutes for me?
I’m not sure when you have to —
Good because this is real fascinating stuff. Oh you did it. What’s the state of the music industry today?

The state of the music industry today — the words that I would like to use is not very cool. And one of them starts with an S. It’s really that bad. But the big guys have done it to themselves. Greed is what messed up the music industry. When you start making profits of, instead of single digits, making profits over the course of the years, what caused them to be as big as they are anyhow, and when you’re making four or five hundred percent in the course of a year, it can mess you totally around. So they just became super, super, giant, giant. And then they started grabbing up everything that they could and not losing anything because there was so much money that they made. Well the problem was, and is, is that too many songs have no melodies. And people who write melodies are not around much anymore. They’re making sounds. Sounds is what’s selling and has been selling in the last ten, fifteen years. Not melodies. So — and don’t get me wrong now — the Rappers have come in and made a name for themselves. But what they did was take from what happened thirty, forty years ago, and they’ve saturated us now to © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-
the point is that people are now tired of hearing the one note, as we used to call it the “One Note Samba.” But the “One Note Samba” has a melody.
Right. And it breaks into a bridge that releases that.

Thank you. Well the way songs are done today and written, nobody can remember any of them. Because it’s all rhythms. Nobody remembers the words. Yeah you have a few of the kids who remember the words. But what it is is that the record people have made millions and millions and millions of dollars on the rappers. So consequently it’s shrinking because people that were rappers twenty, fifteen years ago, are not adult — adults. So you’ve got adult contemporary and they want more. They can’t be that youngster that they were. And then the kids that are growing up with them don’t want them, don’t want the parents with their music, because they want to be something different. Well the kids today are not any different than what it was in the sixties or the seventies or the eighties. The point is is that they’re trying to make their own. They have nothing, so they’re trying to create something from something that was already done and it’s already happened so they’re having problems. So they’re wasting time and money. So they’re not making the big bucks, the two, three, four hundred percent. All of a sudden the profit is coming down to double digits and it’s coming down to single digits again. So consequently the industry is hurting because the people who gobbles the money when they — dividends — are not getting it. They’re making money but the dividends are smaller. So people want to go where there’s bigger, better dividends. I’m sorry, it’s just not out there. Until they go back and now start getting people with melodies, that songs stay and linger for thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred years. Why do you think everything is revival? Look at what happens. Nobody is making money on something new. It’s all about revival.
